note: Where performance pressure sits, and what it is allowed to do. A wall-clock reading is a property of the host at that instant, not of the repository, so it grades and records debt and never refuses a landing. Pressure moves to per-check ceilings, which attribute an overrun to the check that owns it instead of to whoever touched the repository next. A single check past catastrophic_check_seconds is a suspected catastrophe. When catastrophic_confirm_alone is true, the verifier re-runs that check after the shared pool drains and refuses only if the isolated reading also crosses the ceiling. This preserves hard pressure on genuine pathological regressions without treating pooled host contention as proof of code failure. This table grants nothing and settles nothing; scripts/verify.py reads it and conformance/fixtures/verification-budget/cases.json defeats it.

wall_clock.note: Bands run fastest first and each ceiling is inclusive. Past the slowest band the run earns no grade and records DEBT. It does not fail. decisions/0050 measured the same commit passing at 2.674s and failing at 3.233s on two runners of one run; that is the reading this rule refuses to treat as a defect.

check_ceilings.note: Twenty-nine of forty-three checks finish under 0.2s. The default is set at 0.5s so ordinary growth is visible without a routine reading tripping it. A named ceiling overrides the default and is set from the measured cost of that check plus modest headroom, except where Bdo named an aspiration in the 2026-08-27 direction: Asset Service reference tests and repository tooling tests carry the numbers he set, which they presently exceed, so the debt is attributed rather than hidden by a ceiling drawn around it.

catastrophic_note: A pooled check past 30 seconds raises a suspected catastrophe. It is re-run alone after the shared pool drains, and only an isolated reading also past 30 seconds refuses the run. This confirmation became necessary when #148/C0027 observed byte-identical PR #151 code first fail solely because Asset Service reference tests measured 36.667s and Console Service reference tests 32.151s on a hosted Python 3.11 runner, then pass on an immediate rerun with no code change. The original 30-second ceiling remains intact: a check that stays past it in isolation still blocks.

measured.host: Windows, eleven live sessions sharing one working tree
measured.note: Recorded so a later reader can tell a ceiling set from evidence from one set from taste. These are loaded-host numbers and are the pessimistic end; a quiet host and the hosted CI runner both come in faster.
